newsitem.title: PERU: Mudslide in Peruvian Andes buries 250-300 people.
newsitem.headline: Mudslide in Peruvian Andes buries 250-300 people.

text.p: Peruvian rescuers using picks, shovels and their bare hands searched on Wednesday for the bodies of an estimated 250 to 300 peasants buried under a mudslide that swept away two remote Andean villages.

"This is a disaster with very serious consequences. It has literally buried two communities where there were approximately 100 families," President Alberto Fujimori told local radio station Radioprogramas del Peru at the site of the disaster.
"We calculate that there are between 250 and 300 people buried under this immense amount of mud that we are seeing here."
He added that 41 bodies had been recovered by mid-afternoon, although an official at the local headquarters of the rescue operation had earlier put that figure at 47.
Fujimori said there were few survivors from the tragedy and warned there was a "huge mass" of mud at the site that could slide if it rained again.
The mountainside in southeastern Peru collapsed before dawn on Tuesday, burying the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra at its foot with a torrent of mud, earth and rocks.
The few survivors of the tragedy told harrowing stories of the mudslide.

Alejandra Huallya Quispe, 14, said she heard a loud rumbling noise just before 4 a.m. local (0900 GMT) on Tuesday. She grabbed her sister and managed to run out of the house "but it crushed my mother and other sister," she told Reuters.
Fujimori said emergency aid was being flown in and soldiers had been drafted to pull out bodies.
A Reuters correspondent at the village of Kerapata beside the mudslide said Fujimori looked grim-faced, brushed aside most reporters and hugged several weeping villagers.
From a helicopter overhead, a vast swathe of mud could be seen covering the villages where the roofs of some houses could be seen poking through the mud.

Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer, accompanying Fujimori, warned of epidemics among between 250 and 600 families left homeless by the mudslide and other flooding and smaller landslips in the same vicinity.

Civil Defence chief Gen. Homero Nurena who was at the site to direct rescue operations said 18 tonnes of supplies were being brought in including tents, beds, blankets, stoves, shovels and picks and dogs to help in the search.

Most of the bodies will never be discovered, he added. "It's turned into an enormous cemetery. Some bodies are eight to 10 meters (26 feet to 33 feet) under the mud and it's impossible to rescue them," he said.
Congressman Dennis Vargas Marin, who comes from the area and flew in to assess damage, said as many as 350 people had disappeared.

Rescue workers pulled dozens of bodies from the mud, many mutilated by stones. "There were arms, heads, pieces of bodies sticking out of the mud," said one firefighter. "We have tried to dig up the bodies using picks and shovels, but it's been difficult."

Authorities were trying to evacuate Kerapata and another nearby village San Jorge because of the risk of mudslides and Abancay was on alert because of the threat of collapse of snowfields and a lagoon in high mountains above the city.
At a makeshift morgue in nearby Tamburco, fifteen bagged bodies were lined up against a wall beside dozens of candles placed on the floor by mourning family members.
Local leaders urged the government to declare a state of emergency for the devastated area.

Flash floods, mudslides and landslides, known locally as "huaycos", are common in Peru's Andes during the January-March rainy season. But Congressman Jubert Chavez Serrano, who also flew to the scene, said: "It's the worst tragedy of this kind we have seen in many years. We had some big 'huaycos' 20 or 30 years ago, but never like this."
